questions.q: What is step 1 of the four-step method for recording a transaction?
questions.explain: Before anything else, you must figure out what changed — which accounts the transaction actually touches.

questions.q: Dunmore Office Partners pays $300 cash for office supplies. What is the correct journal entry?
options: Debit Supplies Expense $300; Credit Accounts Payable $300
questions.explain: Cash (an asset) decreases, so it's credited. Supplies (also an asset) increases, so it's debited.

questions.q: Dunmore performs $2,500 of consulting work for a client who will pay later. What happens to Accounts Receivable?
options: It decreases, because the client has not yet paid
It is not affected by this transaction at all
It becomes a liability instead of an asset
It increases, because the client now owes the business money
questions.explain: Accounts Receivable is an asset representing amounts owed to the business. Billing a client on account increases it.

questions.q: When Dunmore borrows $15,000 from a bank, which account is credited?
questions.explain: Notes Payable (a liability) increases when the business takes on an obligation to repay, so it's credited. Cash is debited since it increased.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which step of the four-step method requires the most real accounting judgment?
options: Step 1 — correctly identifying which accounts are actually involved
All four steps require equal, minimal judgment
questions.explain: Once accounts are correctly identified, classifying, determining direction, and applying the normal-balance rule are nearly mechanical. Identifying the right accounts is where real judgment lives.
